title: Swagger or substance?
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Melissa Muth Martinez uses a rewatch of Martin Gutmann's TED Talk on celebrated incompetent leaders to ask what good leadership actually looks like. Her argument is that organizations keep rewarding confidence, charisma and projection while overlooking the quieter leaders who build engaged, collaborative teams. She draws on her own experience of working under leaders who were praised for intensity while leaving burnout and disconnection behind them. She then lists familiar examples, such as the manager who avoids hard conversations or the director who talks about empowerment but excludes staff from decisions. The move at the end is to turn the critique into three diagnostic questions about confidence versus competence, what we value and what we reward. Good leadership, she concludes, is about asking better questions, listening and being accountable for impact.
points: Organizations mistake presentation for presence, so voice, ego and poise get promoted ahead of clarity, competence and compassion.
The cost of rewarding swagger shows up downstream in hiring, promotion, culture and morale, not just in meeting performance.
Her concrete examples (the leader who skips hard conversations, the one who never invites staff to the decision table) make the pattern easy to spot in your own workplace.
Stating what you actually value and reward is a prerequisite to getting the collaboration and accountability you claim to want.
quotes: In his work, Gutmann sheds light on a frustrating but seemingly enduring pattern: when it comes to leadership, we reward confidence, command, and charm, rather than clarity, competence, compassion. He explains how history—and, not surprisingly, modern workplaces—are full of leaders who climbed the ranks because they fit the part that speaks to the former. They looked and sounded right.

When leadership is defined by presentation rather than presence, we mistake voice for values, ego for expertise, poise for principle. And this is the stuff that ends up shaping everything—from hiring decisions to promotions to culture and morale—and ultimately, outcomes.

Here at Honest Office, I talk a lot about reducing ambiguity and amplifying clarity: defining what we actually want, expect, and value, not just vaguely talking about it. If we say we want to move towards greater collaboration, transparency, accountability, and impact, but we stick to the same template of rewarding the same stuff—voice, ego, and poise—how can we actually get there?

Think of the leader who speaks with certainty in every meeting, makes decisions quickly, and never admits to being wrong. They’re decisive, without a doubt, but where’s the thoughtfulness behind their choices? And where are the outcomes?

Leadership isn’t about being bold and having all the answers. On the contrary. It’s about asking better questions, listening deeply, and being accountable for our impact—on processes, people, and outcomes.
